1:
The parenthesis about the doors is read as a mark of exactness. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) takes it for a note of historical accuracy, intimating that what had been said earlier about setting up the doors was written by way of anticipation, and he observes that the three ringleaders always have the pre-eminence in these lists. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read the same clause as a parenthetical sentence limiting the statement just made, and gloss the opening verb as an impersonal passive, it was heard by him in the indefinite sense of its coming to his ears, noting that such passives grow more frequent in later Hebrew; the rest of the enemies they identify from an earlier chapter as Ashdodites and other hostile individuals. John Gill (reformed) reads the report at its strongest, that the wall was quite finished.

Where the proposed meeting lay, and what it was for, divides them flatly. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) supposes Ono to have been in the tribe of Benjamin, near Jordan, and says plainly what the invitation was for: they wished to get him out of Jerusalem and away from his friends, that they might either carry him off or murder him. Ellicott sends the reader in the opposite direction, naming a particular village in the plain of Ono and placing that plain on the borders of Philistia, more than twenty miles from Jerusalem; he also notices that Tobiah is dropped from the invitation, appearing only as Sanballat’s secretary. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) gives the pretext rather than the purpose, that they proposed to consult about the common service of their master the king of Persia, or to make a friendly accommodation. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) explains the choice of a village: not any city, lest that should excite a suspicion that they intended to secure him.

The famous answer is admired for what it withholds. Henry notes that Nehemiah says nothing of his jealousies and does not reproach them with their treacherous design, but gives them a good reason, and one of the true reasons, for staying where he was; his care was that the work might not cease, and compliment must always give way to business. Clarke makes the reticence a calculation: though Nehemiah knew their design he did not think it prudent to mention it, for had he done so they would probably have gone to extremities on finding themselves discovered, and perhaps have attacked Jerusalem while it was ill provided, their preference being to work by treachery rather than open violence. Keil and Delitzsch put the reason at its most practical, that he could not undertake the journey because his presence in Jerusalem was necessary to the uninterrupted prosecution of the building. Gill adds a detail of manner: he showed them no open contempt and did not even reply by their own messenger, but sent people of his own.

That the request came four times is taken as evidence of what they really wanted. Henry judges the repeated refusal to have been very vexatious to them, since it was the ceasing of the work they aimed at all along, and it must have made them despair of breaking the undertaking to see the undertaker so intent upon it; from the four attempts he draws the rule that we must never suffer ourselves to be overcome by the greatest importunity to do anything sinful or imprudent, but must meet the same temptation with the same reason and resolution. Wesley repeats that rule almost in Henry’s words. Gill accounts for the persistence simply, that they were very desirous of getting him into their hands and so grew pressing and importunate, while Keil and Delitzsch note only that the phrase for answering them in the same manner has a parallel in the second book of Samuel.
5:
That the fifth letter came unsealed is read three ways. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) takes it for a studied insult to a man of Nehemiah’s quality, since letters sent to chiefs and governors in the East are always folded into costly silken bags and sealed, marking his contempt. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) makes it a change of tactics rather than a slight: the bag was left unsealed in the hope that Nehemiah would be alarmed by the thought that the people had already read what was in it. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the openness as a claim about the contents, as speaking of a thing commonly known. John Gill (reformed) attends instead to the sender, that Sanballat now writes in his own name with neither Tobiah nor Geshem joining him, being more anxious than any of them to get Nehemiah into his hands, and perhaps pretending more friendship than the rest by writing as though they knew nothing of it.

The quoted rumour is taken as evidence that the letter is quoted exactly. Ellicott notices that Nehemiah can reproduce the very document, down to its dialectal change of Geshem into Gashmu, and sets out its machinery: Sanballat represents Geshem as circulating a report which, once it reached the distant king, would be read as rebellion, hints that the nations would side with the king, and refers the prophecies of a future King to Nehemiah’s ambition before proposing friendly counsel to avert the danger. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) confirm the form of the name from the earlier chapter and press the grammar, the participle being used of what a man intends or prepares to do, so that the charge is that he means to become their king, and the particle carrying the sense that for no other reason than rebellion does he build the wall. Gill marks the breadth of the report, that it was no whisper among a few but common talk in divers nations.

On the charge of hiring prophets, Gill makes the sharpest observation: Sanballat said it to cover what he and Tobiah had themselves been doing, tampering with and corrupting and hiring the prophets to discourage Nehemiah and put him upon methods by which the work would cease. Clarke glosses the men as persons pretending a commission to preach and crying that Nehemiah reigneth, and reads the invitation that follows as an order to come and justify himself, which was a trick to get him into Sanballat’s power. Keil and Delitzsch explain the choice of an open letter by the same end, that accusations which anyone might read would oblige Nehemiah to come and clear himself at an interview. Wesley simply renders the letter’s own ostensible sense, that they now had a king of their nation and that the counsel proposed was to examine the matter impartially and clear his innocency.

The closing words raise a textual question. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reports that some read them not as a prayer but as a holy resolution, I will now strengthen my hands, precisely because the address to God is supplied by the translators and not in the text; Christian fortitude, he adds, is sharpened by opposition. Ellicott independently marks the same absence, calling the petition all the more remarkable for the want of the words that have here been inserted, and counts it among the sudden interjectional prayers that abound in the narrative. Keil and Delitzsch rule against the alternative on grammatical ground: the verb is an imperative, and the rendering in the first person of the imperfect, I strengthened, which the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac adopt, is merely an attempt to fit into their context words the translators did not understand. Clarke keeps to the reply itself, that Nehemiah would not trouble himself about a charge his accuser knew to be false.
10:
Where Shemaiah was shut up, and why, is variously reported. John Gill (reformed) offers either his own house or a chamber in the temple, as though he had given himself to meditation, fasting and prayer, or else, as he might have suggested, for safety, designing it as an example; he may have been a priest of the course of Delaiah, and Nehemiah plainly had a good opinion of him, since he went to consult him. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) puts him in a chamber adjoining the temple, on a pretence of singular devotion and communion with God and a further pretence of certain knowledge by the Spirit about the approaching danger. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) thinks him probably a priest, found shut up in his house, who likely sent for the governor and represented himself as in danger from the common enemy.

What the advice would have cost is reckoned up. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) counts two losses at once: the people would have been left without a leader and fallen an easy prey, and Nehemiah, once shut in the temple, would have had his government declared at an end, with Sanballat assuming the reins. Wesley foresees the first of these, that the people would have left their work and every man shifted for his own safety. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) adds that they would have thrown down their arms as well, so that the enemies might have demolished the works; and he reads the deeper aim as mockery, that they meant to bring Nehemiah to do a foolish thing so as to laugh at him and lessen his influence — which is doing the devil’s own work, who tempts men that he may accuse them and draws them into sin that he may glory in their shame. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put it as a legal trap, to seduce him into an illegal step and so give occasion for speaking evil of him.

The refusal itself is read two ways. Four of them hear a point of honour. Gill makes him the king’s commissioner on whom the whole work depended; Clarke has him ask whether he should betray his trust and leave the flock without a shepherd, resolving instead to stand at his post; Wesley presses the same, that the life of the city depended on his presence, and that flight would dishonour God and betray the people; Henry gives the reasoning as, another might flee, but not I. Keil and Delitzsch find a different objection altogether, taking the ambiguous verb not as saving his life but as surviving the act, since Nehemiah had in mind the law that the stranger who comes nigh shall be put to death. Ellicott reaches the same law independently and holds both senses together: first the expression of personal dignity, then of fear, who being as I am, a layman, would go into the temple — and rather than to save his life, he renders it, and live?

Noadiah is put to opposite uses. Clarke would remove her, observing that the Hebrew alone makes the person a prophetess while all the versions but the Arabic read Noadiah the prophet, and judging the final letter a mistake. Ellicott makes her presence the point: a name mentioned nowhere else shows how circumstantial the narrative is, and is indirect evidence of its truth. On the closing appeal they divide again. Gill reads it as asking requital, that God would not only confound and disappoint them but reward them as they deserve. Henry insists it is no imprecation at all, since Nehemiah asks for no particular judgment but refers the cause to him who knows their hearts, whatever injuries are done us being no warrant to avenge ourselves. Ellicott calls it an official prophetic prayer, in which Nehemiah puts God’s own cause into God’s own hands.
15:
Whether a wall could be raised in fifty-two days is defended by three different arguments. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) sees no difficulty in it at all, supposing several thousand workmen, with much of the old wall still entire, the materials at hand and no stones to quarry; and he measures the feat against antiquity, calling it little beside Titus, who threw a wall of five thousand paces round Jerusalem in three days, or Alexander, who walled Alexandria on the Tanais, nearly eight miles in compass, in under thirty days. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) works from the calendar, making the twenty-fifth of Elul about our fifteenth of September and the start therefore late in July, soon after Nehemiah’s arrival, and concludes that with the wall only partly overthrown and the bands of workmen skilfully organised the time is not too short — so that there is no need to adopt the suggestion of Josephus, that the rebuilding took two years and four months. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) adds that they rested on the sabbaths even so, and that the enemies’ threats, meant to weaken them, quickened them instead: out of the eater came forth meat.

That the enemies were cast down in their own eyes is explained from other fallen faces. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note that the phrase occurs nowhere else and must be read beside the falling of Cain’s countenance and the failing of the heart for courage, so that they sank in their own esteem and felt themselves discouraged. Henry reaches the same parallel independently, finding in it envy as much as shame: they were crest-fallen at their own disappointed confidence, and grieved to see Jerusalem walled while the Persian kings had allowed them no such fortifying of the cities of Samaria. Ellicott draws the finer distinction on what the enemies perceived, that the work was wrought of God not miraculously but under divine sanction and help, and observes that by the phrase Nehemiah triumphs over his foes and gives the glory where it was due, his own heroic part being utterly forgotten.

The correspondence of the nobles is taken as the harder trial. Clarke reads these verses as showing what Nehemiah was really up against, enemies without and false friends within, with a treacherous traffic carried on between the nobles of Judah and the Ammonites; and he ventures the judgment that had almost any other man stood at the head of Jewish affairs, Jerusalem would never have been re-established. Henry cannot get past the rank of the offenders, that nobles of Judah had so little sense of honour and of their country’s good, writing with all the freedom and familiarity of friends, from which he concludes only that great men are not always wise nor always honest. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the idiom, that the nobles multiplied their letters.

The oath behind it all is traced to two marriages. Keil and Delitzsch argue, against Bertheau, that the men were associates of an oath, bound to Tobiah personally, and not allies by virtue of a sworn treaty, concluding that the marriage affinity was itself confirmed by an oath; they note that his father-in-law was a respectable Jew of the race of Arah, that his son’s father-in-law was one of the builders, and that Tobiah and his son both bear genuine Hebrew names. Ellicott presses that last point to a conclusion, that though naturalised Ammonites they were probably of Hebrew extraction, which makes the ease of the alliance easier to understand. Henry puts it in a sentence: a sinful love leads to a sinful league. John Gill (reformed) notes that they did not merely correspond but bound themselves by oath to be true to his interest and do as he advised.
